title: I believe in Ubisoft’s plan, but it must get its staff on-side
author: Christopher Dring
excerpt: Plus, four things I loved about the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 launch – Here’s The Dring
text:
The Game Business Show
I believe in Ubisoft’s plan, but it must get its staff on-side
0:00
Current time: 0:00 / Total time: -19:47
-19:47
Paid episode
The full episode is only available to paid subscribers of The Game Business
I believe in Ubisoft’s plan, but it must get its staff on-side
Plus, four things I loved about the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 launch – Here’s The Dring
Christopher Dring
Nov 23 ∙ Paid
Hello! Welcome to another week on The Game Business.
I love the noise and excitement around GTA. And it was obviously the massive story of the week, so we will be talking about that today.
But, there is life outside of Rockstar’s crime opus (believe it or not). And so I’ll begin by chatting about Ubisoft. It’s been a moment.
Enjoy!
Last week, we spoke to former Take-Two and Tencent leader Ben Feder, and we asked him what he would do if he was running a major game publisher today.
He answered: “You need to protect your core, and then grow from there. The core ultimately goes down to your IP, your creative talent, your communities, and your distribution. That’s critically important.”
And that is what most major game publishers are doing. It’s why Xbox closed and sold those studios. It’s why PlayStation backed away from live service. It’s why EA shut BioWare.
And it’s why Ubisoft has been cutting at its business, while forming Vantage Studios. That’s the division it launched a year ago with investment from Tencent. Vantage Studios is the core of Ubisoft. It’s the home of Assassin’s Creed, Far Cry and Rainbow Six. It’s the big brands that deliver, usually, the best results.
The games it has cancelled, the studios it has closed, and the 166 people it laid off last week in Montreal and Quebec, it’s part of protecting that core organization.
Ben Feder suggested that a lot of big companies today are willing to let the startups uncover new IP and new ideas, and when that’s been proven to work, those organizations will spend the money to buy them. Like Take-Two did with Zynga to get into mobile, or Sony did with Bungie to get into live-service. It doesn’t always work, but it can be a safer (albeit more costly) route than over-investing in new developments and risk losing focus on the core business.
But new ideas is in Ubisoft’s DNA. This is the company that jumped first at Nintendo Wii and Kinect and blockchain and VR and now at AI. That desire to try new things and see where it leads is ingrained in the company’s personality.
It’s why Ubisoft has cut, but not at everything. And it’s why I like the Creative House concept, where it’s split the business into multiple different divisions with their own budgets, goals and leadership. By putting all the big brands under one House, it protects that core, and the other Houses allow it to experiment with new ideas and support different scales of IP.
Take for instance Creative House 2, or Massive Entertainment as it’s now called. This is the group that looks after Splinter Cell, Ghost Recon and The Division (plus, new IP March of Giants). It’s run by former 2K and Amazon Games boss Christoph Hartmann. You could call this group ‘the shooters that aren’t as big as Far Cry or Rainbow Six’.

title: AI Update Part 3: The Clone Wars
author: Ross Burton, PhD
text:
AI Update Part 3: The Clone Wars
Share:
Author: Ross Burton, PhD, Head of Product and Data
Category: Data Analysis
Published: 11/23/2026
Updated: 11/23/2026
In late August 2026 a short clip of a game about finding one needle in five million pieces of hay passed 50 million views 1 . Within days, at least eight similarly named games had Steam pages; Kotaku counted more than ten by mid-September 1 . One of them, with a public demo, overtook the original's follower count on 5 October while the original was still running a closed playtest 2 . By October the developers from one of the copies were complaining that their game had been copied too, down to class names and error messages 1 .
Stories like this have made a lot of indie developers nervous about showing their games early. Studios have pulled public demos and playtests because of them. The worry is reasonable and the question I want to ask is just how big is the AI cloning problem on Steam, or, more specifically:
Are tight clusters of near-identical games exploding onto Steam, very recently, in particular corners of the market? At what rate, and where?
Spoiler alert: This phenomenon of AI cloning is concentrated in a small, specific corner of Steam, and the copies mostly don't win.
Before I dive into the analysis, there are few things I want to be up front about. Here are some things this analysis does not do:
It doesn't decide who copied whom. With Needle in a Haystack Simulator, the idea went viral on social media before any Steam page existed, so store data can't tell you who had it first, even though we personally know who the original developer was.
It doesn't accuse anyone. Making a game in a popular niche is legal, and many of these developers may have arrived at the same idea independently.
It measures the phenomenon itself: namely many near-identical pages from different developers arriving together.
Measuring "bursts" of Steam store pages
I tracked nearly 79,000 new Steam pages, looking for groups of similar games appearing unusually close together. To do this I used a clever trick from the world of epidemiology. If that sort of thing interests you, checkout the methodology section at the bottom of this article where I go into all the gritty details.
Throughout this article I'm going to talk about these bursts of store pages. A “burst” means at least five lookalike pages arriving within 60 days, faster than I’d expect even after accounting for Steam’s normal growth. Each group gets a “burst score”: the higher the score, the more unusual the pile-up, not the stronger the proof of copying.
Below, I specifically focus on “multi-developer bursts”. These bursts of store pages are from different developers arriving with the same specific idea or a closely related theme, rather than one studio uploading its back catalogue. I compare rates and shares of new pages, not just raw totals, so Steam getting busier doesn’t automatically look like a cloning epidemic.
Clones have exploded only recently
Throughout 2025, bursts of near-identical pages from several developers were quite rare. I could only find 5 in the whole year. That’s 5 bursts among 28,201 new pages; a rate of 0.18 per 1,000 pages published.
Most of the 2025 bursts were single developers publishing a series ("100 Cats Lost in X", "Sudoku-X") or rights holders re-releasing old games (Rance, Psikyo shoot-'em-ups, Geoff Crammond racing).
That changed abruptly in the summer of 2026. Bursts of near-identicle pages being published around a similar time by multiple different developers increased from 3 bursts in July to 13 in August, 32 in September, and then 27 in October. In the 90 days between 9th August to 6th November, there were 71 bursts among 19,744 new pages. So the rate has now risen to 3.6 per 1,000, which is 20  times the 2025 rate. If identical pages were to be released at a similar time by chance alone, this would produce less than one burst per year.
Bursts of near-identical pages by the month they started, by the type of burst, and with the number expected by chance (dotted white line). November 2026 holds only six days of data, so don’t read into that, but I’ve shown it for transparency. How big is the impact on Steam?
Counting bursts of similar games being released shows that something changed on Steam, but it doesn't show how big the change is, because a burst can hold anything from 5 games to more than 30.
So I decided we needed to also ask a simpler question: what fraction of new store pages between Jan 2025 and Nov 2026 were part of a burst of near-identical pages all coming from different developers?
To make it fair and to not overstate the problem, each page is counted once, even if it sits near more than one burst.
I will give the fraction as a range, because it depends on how strict you are about "near-identical" and that can be very subjective:
The low figure in the range is strict. It counts only bursts of games where several developers published a page about the same specific game idea (e.g. the “finding a needle in a haystack” games).
The high figure in the range is looser. It also counts genre waves, where several developers piled into the same broader theme at the same time.
The table below shows what I found:

So what this basically means is, in October 2026, somewhere between 1 in 20 and 1 in 13  new Steam pages belonged to a group of near-identical pages from different developers, all released within weeks of each other. Throughout the entirety of 2025 it was about one in 450, which is 20-35 times lower.
Share of each month's new pages that were part of a burst from several developers. The red bars show pages sharing one specific idea (the low figure in the table). The red bars plus the purple bars show pages sharing an idea or a broader theme (the high figure). Data for November 2026 was incomplete, so I left it out. To increase my own confidence in these findings, I tried to break it, and the observations hold even when I change each of the following:
The time window: 30 or 90 days instead of 60.
The minimum burst size: 3 or 8 games instead of 5.
The neighbourhood size
The level of similarity: only two of three things need to be similar rather than all of  the text, screenshots or title.
Across these variants, 2026 has between 4 and 30 times as many multi-developer bursts of similar releases as 2025. The findings also hold up when I replaced "the day I first saw a page" with the order in which Steam registered the app. So I can safely say these findings are not an artifact of when our pipeline found pages.
Bursts fill up fast
The fifth page in a burst of similar store pages typically arrives 10 days after the first. The middle half of bursts (the median) takes about 5-14 days and 77% of a burst's store pages arrive within two weeks or less  (n = 86). For example, the “punch-your-way-out-of-walls” burst reached five near-identical store pages within three days!
How fast do these bursts fill-up? On the left, I show the days from a burst's first page to its fifth, and on the right, the total pages within a “burst window” (60 days). Data are shown for 86 multi-developer bursts. Which markets see the most ‘clones’?
It will perhaps be no surprise that these bursts of very similar store pages are not spread evenly across Steam. In the chart below I show how much more common certain themes and genres are amongst “bursts” of very similar store pages compared to other new store pages in a given month:
Tags over- and under-represented among “bursts” of pages, compared with new pages from the same months, with 95% confidence intervals. By theme, the pattern is plain and clear; Tidy-up and sorting sims are the most likely to be copied, with 22 bursts totaling  338 pages. Some examples being are
"Sort Them X" (gnomes, frogs, dogs, alpacas, eggs),
"Tidy Up Together", whether that’s magic shops, archives, game stores, socks…any kind of “sort the thing” game.
Next come four themes with around 110-135 store pages each:
Huge-pile incrementals: needle in a haystack, four-leaf clovers, "one million coins", punch or eat your way out of something
Management sims: niche sports managers, stock trading, etc
Desktop and taskbar idlers: a tiny shop or pet that lives at the bottom of your screen.
Strategy and defence games.
And then smaller waves of mosquito swatting, snow shovelling, booster-pack opening, build-a-computer-from-logic-gates puzzles.
From a glance, what most of these games have in common is a simple loop that's cheap to build. You’re either tasked with putting thousands of things where they belong or the core loop is to do one mundane thing a million times with various challenges sprinkled around it e.g. find one item in an enormous pile.
New pages inside multi-developer bursts, by theme (October 2024 to October 2026). Alt text: Horizontal bar chart in which tidy-up and sorting sims lead with 338 pages, followed by management sims, huge-pile incrementals and desktop idlers at 120 to 135 pages each, down to winter and holiday games at 15. Who is making these games?
The 1,158 pages included in clone bursts come from 1,074 developer identities, and the ten most frequent supply under 5% of all these new pages. So it is not like there are a handful of prolific developers pumping out these new store pages.
If we focus on bursts of pages coming from different developers but focused on the same specific concept and look specifically at the Aug to Oct 2026, they disclose AI use somewhat more often than other new pages, but it’s not as stark as I was expecting:
55% of new pages in a burst disclose AI use versus 49% amongst all other new store pages.
Of those that do disclose the use of AI, they more often disclose AI-generated art and AI store-page assets. These categories come from our disclosure classifier we discussed in Part 1 of this series.
AI disclosure isn't the story here either. Half of the other new pages (the ones that don’t appear in these bursts of very similar store pages) disclose AI too, and several of the “originals” in these bursts disclose AI use as well.
Sidebar: page factories
A separate worry is single developers mass-producing near-identical pages. This was a concern long before AI, but it is a valid concern that AI could make this practice more widespread. People often worry that flooding the store with more pages will make discovery, and therefore commercial success, less obtainable.
For those with that concern I urge you to read our take on this in the first part of this series on AI ; spoiler, the answer is no, more competition does not automatically mean fewer winners.
Despite this, I still think it is interesting to see if AI has in-fact increased the incidence of what I like to call “page factories”. I used 2025 data to define what a page factory is before looking at 2026, just to make it comparable. A developer counts as a factory if both of these are true:
They publish at least five new pages within 90 days.
The store pages they publish read almost the same.
To set the bar, I took every developer with two or more new pages in 2025 (2,232 of them) and measured how similar each developer's store pages were to each other. I ranked those 2,232 developers by how similar their own store pages were to one another. I then set the factory threshold at the point where only the most repetitive 5% of developers qualified, and used that same threshold for 2026.
A busy studio making genuinely different games doesn't count, because its pages aren't alike. Every developer we flagged turned out to be producing template pages, with titles like these:
"100 Anomaly Cats", "100 Snack Cats"
"101 Dogs Hidden in Rome"
"Backrooms: The Void"
"Puzzles: Space Cats"
The surprise is that factories didn't grow in 2026. Like, not at all.
Share of new pages: factory pages accounted for  0.95% of new pages in 2025 and 0.32% in 2026. The 2026 figure rises to 0.67% if I add four renowned template developers our definition missed, a deliberately generous count that still makes no difference.
The classic factory makes hidden-object, jigsaw, sudoku and memory games. That pattern pre-dates the 2026 wave and has nothing to do with AI.
They rarely pile into other developers' bursts. Factory pages appear in only 6 of the 86 multi-developer bursts of similar page releases (1.6% of burst pages), typically a month after the burst began.
One exception: a developer my definition missed published 21 "… Together" sorting and tidy-up pages in 2026, every one disclosing AI, spread across 11 different bursts. Their pages were published a median of 19 days after each burst's first page and was never first. But the associated games only have a median of 7 followers.
Volume doesn't buy attention
One hidden-cats series has a real audience with about 300 followers per page across 43 pages. But most factories' pages sit at a handful of followers. The four template developers my definition missed have a median of 3 followers per page (n = 156 pages). In addition to this, released games from these developers do about as well as any other new game (median of 17.5 followers for template developers against 14 followers for all other developers).

Do the copies win?
I purposefully avoid "original" and "clone" here. Instead I want to ask how attention spreads inside a burst of similar pages.
Attention is lopsided, but not unusually so
In the median burst, the most-followed store page holds 46% of the burst's followers (measured from 86 bursts of similar pages). A closer look and you see that this is the same for random groups of new pages of the same size from the same weeks (47% of new pages that are not part of these bursts of similar pages).
That said, copies don't split an idea's audience evenly: one or two pages get most of the attention and the rest get very little, as with any group of new Steam pages. This does not surprise me in the slightest; it’s the same market dynamic that dominates all of Steam! To re-iterate what I said in part 1 of this series, AI might be new but the market dynamics are the same as ever.
How a burst's followers split between its most-followed page, the next two pages and all the rest, against random groups of new pages of the same size from the same time period. Bars show the average across 86 multi-developer bursts. Early arrivals tend to do better
In 20% of bursts, the most followed page is the first one published  and in 49% of bursts, the most followed page is published within the first quarter of pages.
However, being first isn't enough. If you take the “Needle in a Haystack” games and the eight reported Steam copies, the most-followed page is reportedly a copy of the original concept: Find The Needle gathered 9,461 followers, against the original's 6,131. How To Market A Game attributes that to the copy's public demo, while the original ran a closed playtest 2 .
Compare this to the burst of “Escape the Walls” games though, and you’ll see that nobody broke 100 followers. So right now the data is incredibly noisy and I would urge people to not read too deeply into any particular “hot take”.
Being in a burst isn't a death sentence either
If you compare store pages from the same month with the same main tag, pages that appear in a burst have somewhat more followers compared to a typical new page.
Of those games that have been released, the median follower count for games that appeared in a burst of similar games is 14 compared to the typical median follower count of 5. So it is possible that riding a viral idea brings a little attention, though I must emphasize the word little here, especially when observed in absolute terms.
Bursts burn out
In the ten bursts that were old enough that I could follow them for two months after their initial window, new arrivals in the neighbourhood dropped to a median of zero. In other words, people seem to quickly lose interest in releasing into these viral epicenters.
Maybe it is the sheer competition, the viral backlash, or just because some other new trend comes along and they lose interest. The point is, these don’t appear to be self-sustaining trends.
As a game developer, what can you do?
If you’re a game developer, all of this can be a bit disconcerting to say the least. But I want to finish this blog with some useful advice. Our motto at Game Oracle is “data-driven optimism” and I intend to live up to that motto, because what is the point otherwise?!
With that being said, I am not a lawyer and I don’t claim to know everything about game development. I am just a data scientist and indie dev that loves games. So none of this is legal advice, but I hope it helps.
Know you exposure
If your game is a simple, satisfying loop in a cozy or casual niche (sorting, finding, idling on the desktop, doing something a million times), you're in the corner where these bursts of similar concepts are happening.
If, however, your game has a rich unique story, hand-built levels, or highly-tuned action with deep mechanics, these bursts barely touch you. Remember that about 95% of the last 90 days' new pages were outside any burst.
This is one area where I think our Game Oracle platform can genuinely help you. Our market research tools are designed to help you understand where exactly your concept sits in the market, and in the latest v7.2.0 release we also introduced a “clone radar” that warns you when waves of new store pages are clustering around your idea.
Assume the window is about two weeks
Once an idea is public and catchy, the fifth lookalike typically arrives within 10 days. That is what our data suggests anyway.
Hiding the game doesn't reduce that window. Take the “Needle in a Haystack” copies for example. They followed a social-media clip, not an official demo, so you have to be cautious with virality, especially if your core mechanic is simple enough to copy.
What you control is how quickly players can find and play your concept. Can you release a tight vertical slice and use that to build a community early on? The type of community that will support your concept and original vision?
Be playable, build a community, and don't hide away
The “Needle in a Haystack” story is the clearest example: a copy with a public demo overtook the original with a closed playtest. How To Market A Game's advice is to release a demo early, rather than to “shadow drop” 2 . It can seem scary because releasing a demo feels like offering more for people to copy, but Valve's own advice on this matter, at a developer conference in Busan 3 , was to build a loyal community and make games whose appeal goes beyond an easily copied mechanic. GamesRadar summed it up as not relying on "a single mechanic that someone can easily copy" 4 .
I think the worst thing you can do is just hide your work because there are practical things you can do regarding a demo as well. Make the demo a deliberately limited build, rather than the full game with features locked. Exclude unreleased levels, dialogue, progression tables, unused artwork and development tools. The practical question is: “If someone extracts everything in this download, what have we given them?”
But I also want to go a bit further than this and suggest it’s more than just the game you build but also the effort you put into the players of your game. Build a following that a clone can’t inherit. When a mechanic can be copied in days, it’s your relationship with players and the authenticity of your design that becomes a bigger part of your defence.
Share the decisions behind the game, show the person or team making it, and give players a reason to care about your version beyond the hook. A recognisable developer, a consistent voice, and a community that feels involved gives people reasons to support your original concept. It also helps them recognise it when lookalikes appear.
You don’t need to become an influencer either. It could be as simple as answering questions, sharing progress, and making it easy to follow your work. Community won’t stop someone copying your game, but it gives you something they can’t download from a demo. It builds an established relationship with the people you’re making it for.
Obfuscate the implementation
There are real tools for making shipped code and assets harder to inspect:
In Unity you can build with IL2CPP 5 which converts managed code into C++ and then native machine code. There are also obfuscators 6 that rename classes, methods, and fields, which reduces the useful names in recovered code.
In Godot , you can enable PCK encryption, although Godot warns that this just raises the extraction effort rather than eliminating it completely 7 .
In Unreal Engine , use the packaging encryption options appropriate to your engine version and container format. For .pak workflows, Epic documents index, INI, UAsset-header and full-asset encryption 8 .
For all these solutions you should treat encryption as a speed-bump rather than a complete solution. Godot’s documentation states the underlying limitation clearly: a locally running game must contain the key needed to read its encrypted resources. Encryption can defeat easy unpacking but is not going to defeat a determined reverse engineer.
What about anti-AI images, video, and hidden instructions?
Ignore things like Glaze and Nightshade, since they target a different copying workflow; Glaze is designed to disrupt an image model being fine-tuned to imitate an artist’s style and Nightshade poisons images intended to enter a model’s training data.
For a developer whose immediate concern is someone feeding screenshots to an existing coding assistant, these tools are a poor match to the threat of reverse engineering.
I’d recommend a readable game name or studio mark in promotional footage as an attribution measure. If footage gets reposted, give viewers a chance to find the original. Likewise, distinctive marks in your own artwork can be useful things to look for when investigating suspected asset copying.
I would also not recommend embedding instructions such as “ignore previous instructions” in code, textures or metadata as a production defence. Without repeatable tests against the actual copying workflow it is not a dependable protection layer. Plus the latest frontier models have demonstrated they’re resistant to simple prompt injections like this.
Ending with some balanced advice
Overall, looking at all the advice available online right now, the best guidance to avoid your game being coned appears to be:
Don’t rely on short and shallow gameplay loops/concepts that can be easily cloned unless you can build a dedicated audience. Do your market research and spend time cultivating a unique idea, with either deep narrative or innovative mechanics, that addresses some underserved audience or missed opportunity in a market segment that you’re passionate about. Study competitors, read player reviews, go deep into something.
Ship a demo and run playtests, but do so with a deliberately scoped build. Remove unreleased content, development files, and aspects of your game that are not necessary to test core features.
Use your engine’s practical protections: IL2CPP and optional identifier obfuscation in Unity, properly configured PCK encryption in Godot, or appropriate package encryption in Unreal. These measures can raise the cost of extracting your implementation, but they cannot hide a mechanic shown on the screen. Don’t rely on “anti-AI” image filters or prompt injection techniques. They’re unlikely to work the way you think they will.
Put genuine effort into your marketing and community building. This made all the difference long before AI and the fundamental focus has been and should always be your audience, this has not changed.
I’ve been around statistics, machine learning, and AI now for almost 10 years, long before generative AI was really a thing. The pace of change shocks me every day, but I think there is something that has genuinely not shifted: us, people.
In an age where it seems like anyone can build anything (in the digital world at least) what makes our own creations distinct and meaningful? I think the answer is our own lived experience, the community we build around our stories, and the passion we pour into our creative endeavors. I don’t think you can clone that.
Methodology (for the nerds)
This analysis asks whether unusually large groups of very similar Steam pages are appearing within a short space of time, and whether that pattern has become more common. It measures clusters of store pages, not proven cases of copying or AI use.
The Data
Everything comes from the Game Oracle Steam catalogue as of 7 November 2026.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
New pages. I analysed 78,971 Steam pages first seen by Game Oracle between October 2024 and 6 November 2026, excluding re-listings of older games. A page’s arrival date is the day we first saw it, usually within two or three days of it appearing. These are store-page arrivals, not game release dates.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Similarity. I compared each new page with the whole catalogue using store text, screenshots, and titles. Each page’s “neighbourhood” is the set of games most similar to it across all three views.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Developers. I merged developer names that pointed to the same Steam developer page or website. References to different developers therefore mean different developer identities after this matching, although public records cannot establish every relationship between them.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Traction. Follower counts come from Steam. Any wishlist or sales figures are Game Oracle model estimates, not verified figures supplied by developers.
Detecting outbreaks of cloned games
Epidemiologists looking for disease outbreaks ask: are more cases turning up in this place, at this time, than we would expect from how cases are normally distributed? I borrowed the same approach for Steam pages, using Kulldorff’s space-time permutation scan.
Here, a “case” is a new store page, a “place” is a neighbourhood of similar games, and a potential “outbreak” is an unusually concentrated run of arrivals. I call these outbreaks “bursts” throughout the article. The detector identifies unusual timing among lookalike pages; it does not establish whether anyone copied anyone else.
The detection process works like this:
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Count arrivals. For each neighbourhood, count how many of its new pages arrived within a 60-day window. A candidate burst must contain at least five pages.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Calculate an expectation. Work out how many arrivals that neighbourhood would have received if it had taken its usual share of all new pages appearing during that window. This accounts for both the neighbourhood’s overall activity and changes in the volume of new pages across Steam.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Calculate a burst score. Compare the observed count with that expectation. The score rises when more pages arrive together than expected, with stronger evidence from larger excesses. It measures the unusual concentration of arrivals, not how similar the games are or how likely they are to be copies.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Test against chance. Shuffle arrival dates and rerun the detector, keeping the pages and their similarity relationships unchanged. This shows how many apparent bursts could arise from coincidental timing.
I repeated that final step 200 times and compared the number of bursts found in the real data with the number found after shuffling, across a range of score thresholds.
Bursts detected using real arrival dates compared with shuffled arrival dates, at each burst-score threshold. At the chosen threshold of 10, the real data produces 139 bursts, compared with about four in the shuffled data. I chose a score threshold of 10 to keep the estimated false discovery rate below 5%. At this threshold, the shuffled results imply an estimated false discovery rate of 2.7%: roughly three chance detections for every hundred reported bursts.
Something we have to note is that this is not a guarantee about any individual burst, it is just an estimate across the detected set. It also says nothing about copying: a statistically unusual cluster can still consist of developers independently following the same trend. Lowering the threshold would recover more groups, but would also admit more chance detections.
Checking what the bursts actually contain
Unusual timing alone does not tell us whether a group makes sense. To check that, I assessed all 139 detected bursts alongside the 50 highest-scoring groups that fell below the threshold. These “near-misses” help show what the detector leaves out.
I shuffled the 189 groups together and removed their scores so that the classification step was blind to which groups had passed the threshold. An AI model, Claude Opus 5.5, then classified each group using the pages’ titles, developer identities and short descriptions. I manually spot-checked a handful of groups for obvious errors; this was not a full independent human review.
Each group received one of five labels:
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Concept burst: several developers publishing pages built around one specific idea.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Genre wave: several developers publishing pages within a broader shared theme.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Single-developer batch: one developer publishing many similar pages.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Re-release: a rights holder bringing back a back catalogue.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Not a coherent group: pages with little meaningful connection.
Throughout the article, “multi-developer bursts” means concept bursts and genre waves together. Where I give a stricter measure, it includes concept bursts only. Single-developer batches and re-releases are kept separate rather than counted as evidence of several developers converging on an idea.
Of the detected bursts, 86% were classified as coherent groups (95% confidence interval: 81–91%). That includes coherent single-developer batches and re-releases; it does not mean 86% were clones or multi-developer bursts. Among the near-misses, 58% were also coherent, showing that the threshold excludes some meaningful groups as well as noise.
Comparing periods fairly
Steam became much busier during the study. New pages first observed each month nearly quadrupled, from 2,125 in January 2025 to 8,110 in October 2026. More pages create more opportunities for clusters, even without any change in developers’ behaviour.
New Steam pages first observed each month, October 2024 to October 2026. November 2026 is excluded because its data are incomplete. Monthly volume nearly quadrupled between January 2025 and October 2026, making rates and page shares more useful for comparisons than raw burst counts alone. The detector accounts for this growth by comparing each neighbourhood’s arrivals with its expected share of Steam’s activity during the same window. For comparisons over time, I also report two measures:
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Bursts per 1,000 new pages, rather than relying on raw burst counts.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
The share of each month’s new pages belonging to a multi-developer burst. Each page is counted once, even if it belongs to overlapping bursts.
For the page-share measure, the lower end of the reported range includes only concept bursts. The upper end adds genre waves. This makes the effect of a stricter or broader definition visible, rather than treating “near-identical” as an entirely objective boundary.
Monthly burst counts are assigned to the month in which a burst started. Monthly page shares instead describe the pages first observed in that month. These measures answer different questions: how often bursts begin, and how much of the incoming catalogue they occupy.
Testing whether the result depends on the settings
I reran the analysis with alternative settings:
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Time windows of 30 and 90 days instead of 60.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Minimum burst sizes of three and eight pages instead of five.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Different neighbourhood sizes.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Similarity based on two of the three views instead of requiring all three.
Across these variants, the reported increase in multi-developer bursts from 2025 to 2026 ranged from fourfold to thirtyfold. The size of the increase depends on the settings, but its direction did not.
The pattern also held when I used the order in which Steam registered apps as an alternative to first-observed dates. This reduces the concern that the increase is simply an artefact of when our collection pipeline found pages, although it cannot eliminate every source of timing error.
Caveats and limits
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
A burst is not proof of copying. Developers can independently arrive at similar ideas, respond to the same viral clip or follow the same trend. Store-page timing cannot establish who had an idea first.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
The method does not identify AI-generated games. AI disclosures are analysed separately. Neither similarity nor unusually close timing establishes whether AI was involved.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Store-page similarity is not gameplay similarity. A game that copies mechanics but uses different art, titles and descriptions may not appear in the same neighbourhood. Conversely, similar-looking pages need not contain identical games.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
The counts are not an exhaustive census. The threshold misses coherent groups, and pages removed before they could be captured are absent. At the same time, some detections can occur by chance and some classifications can be wrong.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Classification relied on an AI model. The manual spot-check was limited, and the model worked from titles, developer identities and short descriptions, not a hands-on assessment of every game.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Recent periods are incomplete. November 2026 contains only six days of arrivals, so I exclude it from full-month comparisons. Bursts still forming at the end of the study may not yet meet the detection criteria.
p]:pt-0 [&>p]:mb-2 [&>p]:my-0">
Commercial outcomes are preliminary. Most burst pages have not launched. Followers measure early attention, not sales, and any wishlist or sales estimates remain model-based.

AI Update Part 3: The Clone Wars

Share:
Author: Ross Burton, PhD, Head of Product and Data
Category: Data Analysis
Published: 11/23/2026
Updated: 11/23/2026

In late August 2026 a short clip of a game about finding one needle in five million pieces of hay passed 50 million views1. Within days, at least eight similarly named games had Steam pages; Kotaku counted more than ten by mid-September1. One of them, with a public demo, overtook the original's follower count on 5 October while the original was still running a closed playtest2. By October the developers from one of the copies were complaining that their game had been copied too, down to class names and error messages1.

Stories like this have made a lot of indie developers nervous about showing their games early. Studios have pulled public demos and playtests because of them. The worry is reasonable and the question I want to ask is just how big is the AI cloning problem on Steam, or, more specifically:

Are tight clusters of near-identical games exploding onto Steam, very recently, in particular corners of the market? At what rate, and where?

Spoiler alert: This phenomenon of AI cloning is concentrated in a small, specific corner of Steam, and the copies mostly don't win.

Before I dive into the analysis, there are few things I want to be up front about. Here are some things this analysis does not do:

  • It doesn't decide who copied whom. With Needle in a Haystack Simulator, the idea went viral on social media before any Steam page existed, so store data can't tell you who had it first, even though we personally know who the original developer was.

  • It doesn't accuse anyone. Making a game in a popular niche is legal, and many of these developers may have arrived at the same idea independently.

  • It measures the phenomenon itself: namely many near-identical pages from different developers arriving together.

Measuring "bursts" of Steam store pages

I tracked nearly 79,000 new Steam pages, looking for groups of similar games appearing unusually close together. To do this I used a clever trick from the world of epidemiology. If that sort of thing interests you, checkout the methodology section at the bottom of this article where I go into all the gritty details.

Throughout this article I'm going to talk about these bursts of store pages. A “burst” means at least five lookalike pages arriving within 60 days, faster than I’d expect even after accounting for Steam’s normal growth. Each group gets a “burst score”: the higher the score, the more unusual the pile-up, not the stronger the proof of copying.

Below, I specifically focus on “multi-developer bursts”. These bursts of store pages are from different developers arriving with the same specific idea or a closely related theme, rather than one studio uploading its back catalogue. I compare rates and shares of new pages, not just raw totals, so Steam getting busier doesn’t automatically look like a cloning epidemic.

Clones have exploded only recently

Throughout 2025, bursts of near-identical pages from several developers were quite rare. I could only find 5 in the whole year. That’s 5 bursts among 28,201 new pages; a rate of 0.18 per 1,000 pages published.

Most of the 2025 bursts were single developers publishing a series ("100 Cats Lost in X", "Sudoku-X") or rights holders re-releasing old games (Rance, Psikyo shoot-'em-ups, Geoff Crammond racing).

That changed abruptly in the summer of 2026. Bursts of near-identicle pages being published around a similar time by multiple different developers increased from 3 bursts in July to 13 in August, 32 in September, and then 27 in October. In the 90 days between 9th August to 6th November, there were 71 bursts among 19,744 new pages. So the rate has now risen to 3.6 per 1,000, which is 20  times the 2025 rate. If identical pages were to be released at a similar time by chance alone, this would produce less than one burst per year.

How big is the impact on Steam?

Counting bursts of similar games being released shows that something changed on Steam, but it doesn't show how big the change is, because a burst can hold anything from 5 games to more than 30. 

So I decided we needed to also ask a simpler question: what fraction of new store pages between Jan 2025 and Nov 2026 were part of a burst of near-identical pages all coming from different developers?

To make it fair and to not overstate the problem, each page is counted once, even if it sits near more than one burst.

I will give the fraction as a range, because it depends on how strict you are about "near-identical" and that can be very subjective:

  • The low figure in the range is strict. It counts only bursts of games where several developers published a page about the same specific game idea (e.g. the “finding a needle in a haystack” games).

  • The high figure in the range is looser. It also counts genre waves, where several developers piled into the same broader theme at the same time.

The table below shows what I found:

Period

New pages

Share of store pages inside a multi-developer burst

Frequency of “clones” 

2025 (whole year)

28,201

0.22% (62 pages)

1 in 450

August 2026

5,673

0.9-1.2% (about 50-70 pages)

1 in 80-110

September 2026

5,987

3.3-4.2% (about 200-250 pages)

1 in 24-30

October 2026

8,110

5.1-7.6% (about 410-620 pages)

1 in 13-20

So what this basically means is, in October 2026, somewhere between 1 in 20 and 1 in 13  new Steam pages belonged to a group of near-identical pages from different developers, all released within weeks of each other. Throughout the entirety of 2025 it was about one in 450, which is 20-35 times lower.

To increase my own confidence in these findings, I tried to break it, and the observations hold even when I change each of the following:

  • The time window: 30 or 90 days instead of 60.

  • The minimum burst size: 3 or 8 games instead of 5.

  • The neighbourhood size

  • The level of similarity: only two of three things need to be similar rather than all of  the text, screenshots or title.

Across these variants, 2026 has between 4 and 30 times as many multi-developer bursts of similar releases as 2025. The findings also hold up when I replaced "the day I first saw a page" with the order in which Steam registered the app. So I can safely say these findings are not an artifact of when our pipeline found pages.

Bursts fill up fast

The fifth page in a burst of similar store pages typically arrives 10 days after the first. The middle half of bursts (the median) takes about 5-14 days and 77% of a burst's store pages arrive within two weeks or less  (n = 86). For example, the “punch-your-way-out-of-walls” burst reached five near-identical store pages within three days!

Which markets see the most ‘clones’? 

It will perhaps be no surprise that these bursts of very similar store pages are not spread evenly across Steam. In the chart below I show how much more common certain themes and genres are amongst “bursts” of very similar store pages compared to other new store pages in a given month:

By theme, the pattern is plain and clear; Tidy-up and sorting sims are the most likely to be copied, with 22 bursts totaling  338 pages. Some examples being are 

  • "Sort Them X" (gnomes, frogs, dogs, alpacas, eggs),

  • "Tidy Up Together", whether that’s magic shops, archives, game stores, socks…any kind of “sort the thing” game.

Next come four themes with around 110-135 store pages each:

  • Huge-pile incrementals: needle in a haystack, four-leaf clovers, "one million coins", punch or eat your way out of something

  • Management sims: niche sports managers, stock trading, etc

  • Desktop and taskbar idlers: a tiny shop or pet that lives at the bottom of your screen.

  • Strategy and defence games.

And then smaller waves of mosquito swatting, snow shovelling, booster-pack opening, build-a-computer-from-logic-gates puzzles.

From a glance, what most of these games have in common is a simple loop that's cheap to build. You’re either tasked with putting thousands of things where they belong or the core loop is to do one mundane thing a million times with various challenges sprinkled around it e.g. find one item in an enormous pile.

Who is making these games?

The 1,158 pages included in clone bursts come from 1,074 developer identities, and the ten most frequent supply under 5% of all these new pages. So it is not like there are a handful of prolific developers pumping out these new store pages.

If we focus on bursts of pages coming from different developers but focused on the same specific concept and look specifically at the Aug to Oct 2026, they disclose AI use somewhat more often than other new pages, but it’s not as stark as I was expecting:

  • 55% of new pages in a burst disclose AI use versus 49% amongst all other new store pages. 
  • Of those that do disclose the use of AI, they more often disclose AI-generated art and AI store-page assets. These categories come from our disclosure classifier we discussed in Part 1 of this series.
  • AI disclosure isn't the story here either. Half of the other new pages (the ones that don’t appear in these bursts of very similar store pages) disclose AI too, and several of the “originals” in these bursts disclose AI use as well.

Sidebar: page factories

A separate worry is single developers mass-producing near-identical pages. This was a concern long before AI, but it is a valid concern that AI could make this practice more widespread. People often worry that flooding the store with more pages will make discovery, and therefore commercial success, less obtainable. 

For those with that concern I urge you to read our take on this in the first part of this series on AI; spoiler, the answer is no, more competition does not automatically mean fewer winners.

Despite this, I still think it is interesting to see if AI has in-fact increased the incidence of what I like to call “page factories”. I used 2025 data to define what a page factory is before looking at 2026, just to make it comparable. A developer counts as a factory if both of these are true:

  • They publish at least five new pages within 90 days.

  • The store pages they publish read almost the same. 

To set the bar, I took every developer with two or more new pages in 2025 (2,232 of them) and measured how similar each developer's store pages were to each other. I ranked those 2,232 developers by how similar their own store pages were to one another. I then set the factory threshold at the point where only the most repetitive 5% of developers qualified, and used that same threshold for 2026.

A busy studio making genuinely different games doesn't count, because its pages aren't alike. Every developer we flagged turned out to be producing template pages, with titles like these:

  • "100 Anomaly Cats", "100 Snack Cats"

  • "101 Dogs Hidden in Rome"

  • "Backrooms: The Void"

  • "Puzzles: Space Cats"

The surprise is that factories didn't grow in 2026. Like, not at all.

  • Share of new pages: factory pages accounted for  0.95% of new pages in 2025 and 0.32% in 2026. The 2026 figure rises to 0.67% if I add four renowned template developers our definition missed, a deliberately generous count that still makes no difference.

  • The classic factory makes hidden-object, jigsaw, sudoku and memory games. That pattern pre-dates the 2026 wave and has nothing to do with AI.

  • They rarely pile into other developers' bursts. Factory pages appear in only 6 of the 86 multi-developer bursts of similar page releases (1.6% of burst pages), typically a month after the burst began.

  • One exception: a developer my definition missed published 21 "… Together" sorting and tidy-up pages in 2026, every one disclosing AI, spread across 11 different bursts. Their pages were published a median of 19 days after each burst's first page and was never first. But the associated games only have a median of 7 followers.

Volume doesn't buy attention

One hidden-cats series has a real audience with about 300 followers per page across 43 pages. But most factories' pages sit at a handful of followers. The four template developers my definition missed have a median of 3 followers per page (n = 156 pages). In addition to this, released games from these developers do about as well as any other new game (median of 17.5 followers for template developers against 14 followers for all other developers).

Do the copies win?

I purposefully avoid "original" and "clone" here. Instead I want to ask how attention spreads inside a burst of similar pages.

Attention is lopsided, but not unusually so

In the median burst, the most-followed store page holds 46% of the burst's followers (measured from 86 bursts of similar pages). A closer look and you see that this is the same for random groups of new pages of the same size from the same weeks (47% of new pages that are not part of these bursts of similar pages). 

That said, copies don't split an idea's audience evenly: one or two pages get most of the attention and the rest get very little, as with any group of new Steam pages. This does not surprise me in the slightest; it’s the same market dynamic that dominates all of Steam! To re-iterate what I said in part 1 of this series, AI might be new but the market dynamics are the same as ever.

Early arrivals tend to do better

In 20% of bursts, the most followed page is the first one published  and in 49% of bursts, the most followed page is published within the first quarter of pages.

However, being first isn't enough. If you take the “Needle in a Haystack” games and the eight reported Steam copies, the most-followed page is reportedly a copy of the original concept: Find The Needle gathered 9,461 followers, against the original's 6,131. How To Market A Game attributes that to the copy's public demo, while the original ran a closed playtest2. 

Compare this to the burst of “Escape the Walls” games though, and you’ll see that nobody broke 100 followers. So right now the data is incredibly noisy and I would urge people to not read too deeply into any particular “hot take”.

Being in a burst isn't a death sentence either

If you compare store pages from the same month with the same main tag, pages that appear in a burst have somewhat more followers compared to a typical new page. 

Of those games that have been released, the median follower count for games that appeared in a burst of similar games is 14 compared to the typical median follower count of 5. So it is possible that riding a viral idea brings a little attention, though I must emphasize the word little here, especially when observed in absolute terms.

Bursts burn out

In the ten bursts that were old enough that I could follow them for two months after their initial window, new arrivals in the neighbourhood dropped to a median of zero. In other words, people seem to quickly lose interest in releasing into these viral epicenters. 

Maybe it is the sheer competition, the viral backlash, or just because some other new trend comes along and they lose interest. The point is, these don’t appear to be self-sustaining trends.

As a game developer, what can you do?

If you’re a game developer, all of this can be a bit disconcerting to say the least. But I want to finish this blog with some useful advice. Our motto at Game Oracle is “data-driven optimism” and I intend to live up to that motto, because what is the point otherwise?!

With that being said, I am not a lawyer and I don’t claim to know everything about game development. I am just a data scientist and indie dev that loves games. So none of this is legal advice, but I hope it helps.

Know you exposure

If your game is a simple, satisfying loop in a cozy or casual niche (sorting, finding, idling on the desktop, doing something a million times), you're in the corner where these bursts of similar concepts are happening. 

If, however, your game has a rich unique story, hand-built levels, or highly-tuned action with deep mechanics, these bursts barely touch you. Remember that about 95% of the last 90 days' new pages were outside any burst.

This is one area where I think our Game Oracle platform can genuinely help you. Our market research tools are designed to help you understand where exactly your concept sits in the market, and in the latest v7.2.0 release we also introduced a “clone radar” that warns you when waves of new store pages are clustering around your idea.

Assume the window is about two weeks

Once an idea is public and catchy, the fifth lookalike typically arrives within 10 days. That is what our data suggests anyway. 

Hiding the game doesn't reduce that window. Take the “Needle in a Haystack” copies for example. They followed a social-media clip, not an official demo, so you have to be cautious with virality, especially if your core mechanic is simple enough to copy. 

What you control is how quickly players can find and play your concept. Can you release a tight vertical slice and use that to build a community early on? The type of community that will support your concept and original vision?

Be playable, build a community, and don't hide away

The “Needle in a Haystack” story is the clearest example: a copy with a public demo overtook the original with a closed playtest. How To Market A Game's advice is to release a demo early, rather than to “shadow drop”2. It can seem scary because releasing a demo feels like offering more for people to copy, but Valve's own advice on this matter, at a developer conference in Busan3, was to build a loyal community and make games whose appeal goes beyond an easily copied mechanic. GamesRadar summed it up as not relying on "a single mechanic that someone can easily copy"4.

I think the worst thing you can do is just hide your work because there are practical things you can do regarding a demo as well. Make the demo a deliberately limited build, rather than the full game with features locked. Exclude unreleased levels, dialogue, progression tables, unused artwork and development tools. The practical question is: “If someone extracts everything in this download, what have we given them?”

But I also want to go a bit further than this and suggest it’s more than just the game you build but also the effort you put into the players of your game. Build a following that a clone can’t inherit. When a mechanic can be copied in days, it’s your relationship with players and the authenticity of your design that becomes a bigger part of your defence. 

Share the decisions behind the game, show the person or team making it, and give players a reason to care about your version beyond the hook. A recognisable developer, a consistent voice, and a community that feels involved gives people reasons to support your original concept. It also helps them recognise it when lookalikes appear.

You don’t need to become an influencer either. It could be as simple as answering questions, sharing progress, and making it easy to follow your work. Community won’t stop someone copying your game, but it gives you something they can’t download from a demo. It builds an established relationship with the people you’re making it for.

Obfuscate the implementation

There are real tools for making shipped code and assets harder to inspect:

  • In Unity you can build with IL2CPP5 which converts managed code into C++ and then native machine code. There are also obfuscators6 that rename classes, methods, and fields, which reduces the useful names in recovered code.

  • In Godot, you can enable PCK encryption, although Godot warns that this just raises the extraction effort rather than eliminating it completely7. 

  • In Unreal Engine, use the packaging encryption options appropriate to your engine version and container format. For .pak workflows, Epic documents index, INI, UAsset-header and full-asset encryption8.

For all these solutions you should treat encryption as a speed-bump rather than a complete solution. Godot’s documentation states the underlying limitation clearly: a locally running game must contain the key needed to read its encrypted resources. Encryption can defeat easy unpacking but is not going to defeat a determined reverse engineer.

What about anti-AI images, video, and hidden instructions?

Ignore things like Glaze and Nightshade, since they target a different copying workflow; Glaze is designed to disrupt an image model being fine-tuned to imitate an artist’s style and Nightshade poisons images intended to enter a model’s training data.

For a developer whose immediate concern is someone feeding screenshots to an existing coding assistant, these tools are a poor match to the threat of reverse engineering.

I’d recommend a readable game name or studio mark in promotional footage as an attribution measure. If footage gets reposted, give viewers a chance to find the original. Likewise, distinctive marks in your own artwork can be useful things to look for when investigating suspected asset copying. 

I would also not recommend embedding instructions such as “ignore previous instructions” in code, textures or metadata as a production defence. Without repeatable tests against the actual copying workflow it is not a dependable protection layer. Plus the latest frontier models have demonstrated they’re resistant to simple prompt injections like this.

Ending with some balanced advice

Overall, looking at all the advice available online right now, the best guidance to avoid your game being coned appears to be:

  • Don’t rely on short and shallow gameplay loops/concepts that can be easily cloned unless you can build a dedicated audience. Do your market research and spend time cultivating a unique idea, with either deep narrative or innovative mechanics, that addresses some underserved audience or missed opportunity in a market segment that you’re passionate about. Study competitors, read player reviews, go deep into something.

  • Ship a demo and run playtests, but do so with a deliberately scoped build. Remove unreleased content, development files, and aspects of your game that are not necessary to test core features.

  • Use your engine’s practical protections: IL2CPP and optional identifier obfuscation in Unity, properly configured PCK encryption in Godot, or appropriate package encryption in Unreal. These measures can raise the cost of extracting your implementation, but they cannot hide a mechanic shown on the screen. Don’t rely on “anti-AI” image filters or prompt injection techniques. They’re unlikely to work the way you think they will.

  • Put genuine effort into your marketing and community building. This made all the difference long before AI and the fundamental focus has been and should always be your audience, this has not changed. 

I’ve been around statistics, machine learning, and AI now for almost 10 years, long before generative AI was really a thing. The pace of change shocks me every day, but I think there is something that has genuinely not shifted: us, people. 

In an age where it seems like anyone can build anything (in the digital world at least) what makes our own creations distinct and meaningful? I think the answer is our own lived experience, the community we build around our stories, and the passion we pour into our creative endeavors. I don’t think you can clone that.

Methodology (for the nerds)

This analysis asks whether unusually large groups of very similar Steam pages are appearing within a short space of time, and whether that pattern has become more common. It measures clusters of store pages, not proven cases of copying or AI use.

The Data

Everything comes from the Game Oracle Steam catalogue as of 7 November 2026.

  • New pages. I analysed 78,971 Steam pages first seen by Game Oracle between October 2024 and 6 November 2026, excluding re-listings of older games. A page’s arrival date is the day we first saw it, usually within two or three days of it appearing. These are store-page arrivals, not game release dates.

  • Similarity. I compared each new page with the whole catalogue using store text, screenshots, and titles. Each page’s “neighbourhood” is the set of games most similar to it across all three views.

  • Developers. I merged developer names that pointed to the same Steam developer page or website. References to different developers therefore mean different developer identities after this matching, although public records cannot establish every relationship between them.

  • Traction. Follower counts come from Steam. Any wishlist or sales figures are Game Oracle model estimates, not verified figures supplied by developers.

Detecting outbreaks of cloned games

Epidemiologists looking for disease outbreaks ask: are more cases turning up in this place, at this time, than we would expect from how cases are normally distributed? I borrowed the same approach for Steam pages, using Kulldorff’s space-time permutation scan.

Here, a “case” is a new store page, a “place” is a neighbourhood of similar games, and a potential “outbreak” is an unusually concentrated run of arrivals. I call these outbreaks “bursts” throughout the article. The detector identifies unusual timing among lookalike pages; it does not establish whether anyone copied anyone else.

The detection process works like this:

  1. Count arrivals. For each neighbourhood, count how many of its new pages arrived within a 60-day window. A candidate burst must contain at least five pages.

  2. Calculate an expectation. Work out how many arrivals that neighbourhood would have received if it had taken its usual share of all new pages appearing during that window. This accounts for both the neighbourhood’s overall activity and changes in the volume of new pages across Steam.

  3. Calculate a burst score. Compare the observed count with that expectation. The score rises when more pages arrive together than expected, with stronger evidence from larger excesses. It measures the unusual concentration of arrivals, not how similar the games are or how likely they are to be copies.

  4. Test against chance. Shuffle arrival dates and rerun the detector, keeping the pages and their similarity relationships unchanged. This shows how many apparent bursts could arise from coincidental timing.

I repeated that final step 200 times and compared the number of bursts found in the real data with the number found after shuffling, across a range of score thresholds.

I chose a score threshold of 10 to keep the estimated false discovery rate below 5%. At this threshold, the shuffled results imply an estimated false discovery rate of 2.7%: roughly three chance detections for every hundred reported bursts.

Something we have to note is that this is not a guarantee about any individual burst, it is just an estimate across the detected set. It also says nothing about copying: a statistically unusual cluster can still consist of developers independently following the same trend. Lowering the threshold would recover more groups, but would also admit more chance detections.

Checking what the bursts actually contain

Unusual timing alone does not tell us whether a group makes sense. To check that, I assessed all 139 detected bursts alongside the 50 highest-scoring groups that fell below the threshold. These “near-misses” help show what the detector leaves out.

I shuffled the 189 groups together and removed their scores so that the classification step was blind to which groups had passed the threshold. An AI model, Claude Opus 5.5, then classified each group using the pages’ titles, developer identities and short descriptions. I manually spot-checked a handful of groups for obvious errors; this was not a full independent human review.

Each group received one of five labels:

  • Concept burst: several developers publishing pages built around one specific idea.

  • Genre wave: several developers publishing pages within a broader shared theme.

  • Single-developer batch: one developer publishing many similar pages.

  • Re-release: a rights holder bringing back a back catalogue.

  • Not a coherent group: pages with little meaningful connection.

Throughout the article, “multi-developer bursts” means concept bursts and genre waves together. Where I give a stricter measure, it includes concept bursts only. Single-developer batches and re-releases are kept separate rather than counted as evidence of several developers converging on an idea.

Of the detected bursts, 86% were classified as coherent groups (95% confidence interval: 81–91%). That includes coherent single-developer batches and re-releases; it does not mean 86% were clones or multi-developer bursts. Among the near-misses, 58% were also coherent, showing that the threshold excludes some meaningful groups as well as noise.

Comparing periods fairly

Steam became much busier during the study. New pages first observed each month nearly quadrupled, from 2,125 in January 2025 to 8,110 in October 2026. More pages create more opportunities for clusters, even without any change in developers’ behaviour.

The detector accounts for this growth by comparing each neighbourhood’s arrivals with its expected share of Steam’s activity during the same window. For comparisons over time, I also report two measures:

  • Bursts per 1,000 new pages, rather than relying on raw burst counts.

  • The share of each month’s new pages belonging to a multi-developer burst. Each page is counted once, even if it belongs to overlapping bursts.

For the page-share measure, the lower end of the reported range includes only concept bursts. The upper end adds genre waves. This makes the effect of a stricter or broader definition visible, rather than treating “near-identical” as an entirely objective boundary.

Monthly burst counts are assigned to the month in which a burst started. Monthly page shares instead describe the pages first observed in that month. These measures answer different questions: how often bursts begin, and how much of the incoming catalogue they occupy.

Testing whether the result depends on the settings

I reran the analysis with alternative settings:

  • Time windows of 30 and 90 days instead of 60.

  • Minimum burst sizes of three and eight pages instead of five.

  • Different neighbourhood sizes.

  • Similarity based on two of the three views instead of requiring all three.

Across these variants, the reported increase in multi-developer bursts from 2025 to 2026 ranged from fourfold to thirtyfold. The size of the increase depends on the settings, but its direction did not.

The pattern also held when I used the order in which Steam registered apps as an alternative to first-observed dates. This reduces the concern that the increase is simply an artefact of when our collection pipeline found pages, although it cannot eliminate every source of timing error.

Caveats and limits

  • A burst is not proof of copying. Developers can independently arrive at similar ideas, respond to the same viral clip or follow the same trend. Store-page timing cannot establish who had an idea first.

  • The method does not identify AI-generated games. AI disclosures are analysed separately. Neither similarity nor unusually close timing establishes whether AI was involved.

  • Store-page similarity is not gameplay similarity. A game that copies mechanics but uses different art, titles and descriptions may not appear in the same neighbourhood. Conversely, similar-looking pages need not contain identical games.

  • The counts are not an exhaustive census. The threshold misses coherent groups, and pages removed before they could be captured are absent. At the same time, some detections can occur by chance and some classifications can be wrong.

  • Classification relied on an AI model. The manual spot-check was limited, and the model worked from titles, developer identities and short descriptions, not a hands-on assessment of every game.

  • Recent periods are incomplete. November 2026 contains only six days of arrivals, so I exclude it from full-month comparisons. Bursts still forming at the end of the study may not yet meet the detection criteria.

  • Commercial outcomes are preliminary. Most burst pages have not launched. Followers measure early attention, not sales, and any wishlist or sales estimates remain model-based.
